newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian study doubts genetic AIDS protection.
newsitem.headline: Australian study doubts genetic AIDS protection.

text.p: Australian researchers on Friday said they had found evidence which casts doubt on earlier medical findings that a genetic mutation could offer some people protection from the virus that causes AIDS.

A research team from Sydney's Westmead Hospital has reported in the U.S. journal Nature Medicine that they had found a man infected with the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) despite the presence of a genetic mutation which was thought to offer protection against HIV.

Researchers in the United States reported last August that a genetic mutation found in about one percent of Caucasians may confer resistance to HIV, the virus that causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
Those people had a genetic mutation of a receptor known as CCR5 on the membrane of white blood cells.
Everyone carries two copies of the genetic recipe for making CCR5 but it was found that, when both copies were defective, the virus was unable to enter and infect cells.
The latest finding means that not every person with the CCR5 mutation is safe from infection.
"What we're saying is that, like most things in life, never say never," Dr Graeme Stewart, a member of Westmead Hospital's clinical immunology department, told Reuters.
"What we're saying is it's still true, but it doesn't necessarily apply to every single (case). Protection is not complete," he said.
Stewart said his team's discovery had significant implications for pharmaceutical industries that were now working on vaccines and drugs based on the earlier finding.
"The pharmaceutical industry in the U.S. has gone into overdrive moving towards vaccine strategies and treatments that target the CCR5 (mutation)," he said.
"They still should do it, but now they have to keep in their sights the fact that, in some people, the virus can get in through another door," Stewart said.
He said his colleagues would now try to determine how the man, who was diagnosed as HIV-positive in 1992 but is yet to show AIDS symptoms, contracted the virus.
"If we knew that, we could target methods for vaccine studies," he said.
The new finding could also affect people who knew they carried they mutation and thought they were immune to the virus and thus may have stopped practising safe sex.
